title: Google Docs
brief: Design a system like Google Docs: a document in the browser that many people edit at the same moment, with everyone seeing the same text a fraction of a second later. The hard part is not storing text. It is merging simultaneous edits without losing anyone's work.

functional: Create, open and edit a rich text document.
Several people edit the same document live and see each other's changes and cursors.
Keep editing offline and merge when the connection returns.
Share a document with view, comment or edit access.

nonFunctional.name: Latency
nonFunctional.target: A keystroke shows on other screens within 200 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Convergence
nonFunctional.target: After edits stop, every client shows exactly the same document

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: An acknowledged edit is never lost

nonFunctional.name: Local feel
nonFunctional.target: Your own typing appears instantly, never waiting for the server

estimate.note: All figures are assumptions, not facts. The numbers that matter are not total documents but documents being edited right now, because each one needs a live session. An operation is a small edit such as insert a character at position 12.

inputs.label: Operations per second per document
inputs.note: All editors added together, after batching keystrokes.

outputs.label: Live sessions
outputs.note: One collaboration session per document being edited.

outputs.label: Broadcast messages per second
outputs.note: Each operation goes to every other editor.

outputs.label: Log per busy document per day
outputs.note: Assumes one busy hour of editing in the day.

outputs.label: Log to replay on open, at most
outputs.note: Snapshot plus this tail rebuilds the document.

api.does: Checks access, then returns the latest snapshot and the operations after it, plus the revision number.
Opens a socket to the document's session. The server sends anything after rev.
Sends one operation made against baseRev. The server orders it, adjusts it and acknowledges the new revision.
Sends where the cursor is. It is shown to others and never stored.
Grants view, comment or edit access.
Lists named versions and automatic checkpoints. A restore creates a new revision.

data.store: Append-only log, partition key docId, sorted by rev.
data.why: Edits are only ever appended and read in order. The rev gives a total order for one document.

data.store: Object storage keyed by docId and rev.
data.why: A full copy at a known revision. Opening is snapshot plus a short tail of operations.
Small record looked up by id. Not on the typing path.
Two questions: who can open this, and which documents are shared with me.

evolution.title: Save the whole document
evolution.problem: Start with what works: the browser loads a document and saves the entire text back to a server when you pause.
evolution.change: A document service reads and writes one stored copy of the document. Fine for one person at a time.

evolution.title: Send operations, not documents
evolution.problem: Two people save whole copies and the later save silently erases the earlier edits. A save also resends the whole text for one typed letter.
evolution.change: Each edit becomes a small operation, for example insert 'a' at 12, sent over a WebSocket with the revision it was made against. Your own screen applies it at once.
evolution.numbers: about 100 bytes per operation instead of the whole document

evolution.title: One session per document
evolution.problem: With many servers, two edits to the same document can land on different ones. No machine sees them in a single order, so copies drift apart.
evolution.change: A router maps each document id to one session server (consistent hashing). All edits for that document pass through it, it gives them a revision number, adjusts concurrent ones and broadcasts the result.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows how many live sessions exist

evolution.title: Operation log and snapshots
evolution.problem: Saving the document after every operation is slow, a crash would lose recent edits, and there is no history. Replaying a very long log on open is slow too.
evolution.change: The session first appends each operation to a durable log, then acknowledges. A worker writes a snapshot every N operations. Opening loads the latest snapshot and replays the short tail.
evolution.numbers: snapshot interval times bytes per operation is the replay size

evolution.title: Cursors and presence
evolution.problem: People want to see who is here and where they are typing. Cursor moves are far more frequent than edits and must not fill the log.
evolution.change: Cursors and selections travel through the same session but go to a small in-memory presence store, only broadcast and never logged. Losing them costs nothing.

evolution.title: Sharing and access checks
evolution.problem: A shared link must not open to everyone, and removing someone must stop their live edits, not just future page loads.
evolution.change: The gateway checks the permission store when a socket opens and again when access changes, and closes sockets that lose access. Roles are view, comment, edit.

evolution.title: Version history
evolution.problem: Users want to see who changed what and to undo a bad day. Snapshots alone are too coarse.
evolution.change: A history service reads the log and snapshots to rebuild any revision and group edits into readable versions. Restore writes a new revision on top, so nothing is erased.

steps.say: You type. Your browser applies it to your screen at once and builds an operation tagged with the revision it was based on.
The operation goes down the already open WebSocket to an edit gateway.
The gateway asks the router which server owns this document.
The router forwards the operation to that document's session.
The session adjusts it against any operations it accepted since your base revision, then assigns the next revision number.
It appends the operation to the log. Only now is it durable.
It broadcasts the adjusted operation back through the gateway to everyone, including an acknowledgement to you.
The snapshotter notices N operations since the last snapshot and writes a new one.
You open the document. The service checks the latest snapshot and the log tail.
It loads the snapshot, then replays the operations after it, and returns the text with its revision, say 120.
The connection drops. You keep typing. Edits apply locally and queue up, all based on revision 120.
The network returns. The browser reconnects and says 'I am at revision 120, with these queued operations'.
The gateway checks your access has not been removed.
The session sees the document is at 135. It adjusts your queued operations against revisions 121 to 135.
The adjusted operations are appended as 136 and up. Your screen is sent the 15 you missed and applies them.

deepDives.title: Operational transformation or CRDT
deepDives.question: Two people edit at once. How do we merge so both end with the same text?

options.name: Operational transformation
options.pros: A central server picks the order and rewrites each operation to fit what came before. Operations stay small. Simple to reason about with one order.
options.cons: Needs that central server. Getting the rewrite rules right for rich text is famously hard.

options.name: CRDT
options.pros: Every character gets a unique id, so edits merge in any order with no server. Great for peer-to-peer and long offline stretches.
options.cons: Metadata per character, so documents grow. Deleted text leaves tombstones that need cleaning.

options.name: Lock a paragraph
options.pros: Trivial to build. No merge logic.
options.cons: People cannot type in the same paragraph. Feels broken for live collaboration.

deepDives.pick: A central session that orders operations (OT style)
deepDives.because: We already pin one server per document, so a central order is free. That keeps operations small and the log simple. A CRDT is the better choice if offline or peer-to-peer matters most.

deepDives.title: Where the session lives
deepDives.question: How do all edits for one document reach one place?

options.name: Any server, lock in a database
options.cons: Every keystroke fights for a lock and waits on the database. Latency is too high.

options.name: Pin the document to one server
options.pros: Ordering is a counter in memory. Fast. Broadcast stays local.
options.cons: That server is a single point per document. Hot documents cannot be split.

options.name: Pin, with a standby
options.pros: As above, and the log lets another server take over by replaying from the last revision.
options.cons: Needs a router, failure detection and care that two servers never own one document.

deepDives.pick: Pin with a standby, recovered from the log
deepDives.because: One writer per document is the whole trick. A document has a few dozen editors at most, so one server is plenty. The durable log means the session itself holds no truth, so it can be rebuilt.

deepDives.title: Log and snapshots
deepDives.question: How do we store a document that changes thousands of times?

options.name: Only the latest text
options.cons: No history, no recovery from a bad write, no way to merge a late operation.

options.name: Only the log
options.cons: Opening replays everything. Long documents open slowly.

options.name: Log plus periodic snapshots
options.pros: Open is snapshot plus a short tail. History is kept and old log can move to cheaper storage.
options.cons: Snapshots cost extra storage and need a job to produce them.

deepDives.because: Choose the interval so the tail replay is a few hundred operations. Shorter intervals cost more storage, longer ones cost slower opens. The estimator shows the trade.

deepDives.title: Presence and cursors
deepDives.question: How do we show where other people are without drowning the system?

options.name: Treat cursors as operations
options.pros: One mechanism. They stay in order with the text.
options.cons: They bloat the log and slow replay for no value.

options.name: Ephemeral side channel
options.pros: Throttled, not stored, small. A lost cursor update fixes itself on the next one.
options.cons: Cursor positions need adjusting when text moves, so they may briefly lag.

deepDives.pick: Ephemeral side channel, throttled to a few per second
deepDives.because: Cursors are only useful for a moment. Send them through the session but keep them out of the log, and expire a person after missed heartbeats.

failures.impact: Everyone editing its documents is disconnected for a moment.
failures.fix: The router reassigns the documents. The new server replays the log from the latest snapshot, and clients reconnect with their last revision and resend unacknowledged operations.

failures.what: Two servers both think they own a document
failures.impact: Operations get two different orders and copies diverge.
failures.fix: Use a lease with a fencing token. The log only accepts an append from the current owner, and rejects stale ones.

failures.what: A client resends an operation after a lost ack
failures.impact: The same edit is applied twice and a letter doubles.
failures.fix: Each operation carries a client id and a counter. The session ignores any it has already accepted.

failures.what: A document gets enormous or very busy
failures.impact: One session server runs out of memory or CPU, and broadcasts slow.
failures.fix: Cap editors per document, move old content to snapshots, and stop sending presence updates above a threshold. Large audiences get read-only viewers.

failures.impact: A person still holds an open socket and keeps typing.
failures.fix: Permission changes publish an event. The gateway closes the socket, and the session rejects operations from that user.

scaling.lever: Scale by adding session servers. Shard documents by id with consistent hashing, since documents are independent.
Add gateways, as with any chat system. The router holds the mapping, so gateways stay interchangeable.

scaling.limit: Log and snapshot storage grows forever
scaling.lever: Compact old log segments into snapshots and move them to cold storage. Keep recent ones hot.
Place each document's session near most of its editors. Remote editors pay one round trip, and their own typing stays instant.

recap.key: Send small operations to one session per document that gives them a single order, store them in an append-only log with snapshots, and let each screen apply your own edits instantly.
recap.numbers: Assumed: 1B documents, 0.05% active is 500K live sessions, about 1.5M operations per second and 1.5M sockets. A busy document makes about 1 MB of log per day.
moves: One session server per document gives a total order
Append-only log plus snapshots every N operations
Cursors on an ephemeral channel, access checked at the gateway
